articles.headline: New Windows 11 update fixes File Explorer menu mess – and patches an exploited flaw
keyFacts: The November Windows 11 update introduces a customizable File Explorer right-click menu and a new Cloud rebuild recovery option.
Microsoft stated that the monthly update resolves 1,094 security vulnerabilities, including one exploited Outlook spoofing flaw.
Users can check for the mandatory update in Settings and must reboot their computers to complete the installation process.
body: ZDNET’s key takeaways
- You can now customize the right-click menu in Windows 11.
- The new Cloud rebuild can recover Windows if it won’t load.
- The new update supports only Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2.

Windows 11 users who’ve struggled to navigate and use the right-click menu in File Explorer now finally have some relief. With the November Patch Tuesday Windows update, you’re now able to customize the menu to add and remove specific commands and apps so that only your favorites appear.

As usual, the monthly update is mandatory, which means it should automatically download and install on your PC. To check, head to Settings and select Windows Update. If the latest update — labeled “2026-11 Security Update (KB5132061) (26300.9974)” -– pops up as installed with a pending restart, just reboot your computer. Otherwise, click the button to check for updates and allow it to download and install.
More from ZDNET

One caveat: Microsoft’s monthly updates fully support Windows 11 26H2 and 25H2. But support for 24H2 ended last month, at least for the Home and Pro editions. Windows 11 24H2 Enterprise and Education will continue to get monthly security updates, though not regular non-security preview updates, while Windows 11 23H2 Enterprise and Education will receive no more updates after this month.
File Explorer gets a customizable right-click menu
First and foremost in the latest update is the new customizable right-click menu.

The context-sensitive right-click menu is a handy way to quickly access key settings, features, and apps, both in File Explorer and on the desktop. But there’s always been a flaw in its basic design. The more apps you install, the more cluttered and disorganized the menu becomes. That was especially problematic in previous versions of Windows. The old-style, classic menu would grow so long that it would be difficult to navigate and let you find the item you wanted.

With Windows 11, Microsoft introduced a more modern and pared-down menu. But this version can also get crowded. Plus, it may not display every command you need, so you often have to revert to the older classic menu. You’re then stuck dealing with two separate versions of the same menu, leading to an even more confusing and cumbersome experience.

The ideal solution is a menu that you can customize yourself, and that’s what we now have, at least that’s what is now rolling out. Microsoft calls this one a gradual rollout, which means you may or may not get it right away.

To see if and how this is available, open File Explorer and right-click on a folder or file. If the new menu has reached your PC, you’ll see an entry for Customize menu. Select that to view all the available options for tweaking it. Alternatively, head to Settings, select Personalization, and then click the entry for Context menu.

There, you’re able to turn certain file actions on or off, such as Send to, Print, Create shortcut, Copy as path, and Rotate image. You can also choose which apps appear all the time, either in the main menu or in a submenu. Plus, additional options let you decide where certain commands and actions appear and whether you can still access the old-style menu.
Cloud rebuild rolls out
Though the customizable right-click menu is the star of the update, Microsoft has added other surprises as it strives to make Windows more reliable and user-friendly.

Also gradually rolling out, Cloud rebuild is a new recovery option that lets you reinstall Windows 11 via cloud-based system images and drivers downloaded from Windows Update. This tool can help you recover Windows when it won’t load and you don’t have a USB drive or your own custom image. The downside is that your files won’t survive. But if you regularly back them up as you should, you can restore them after Windows is back in business.

To start Cloud rebuild, go to Settings, select System, click Recovery, and then select Rebuild PC. Your PC will then restart into the Windows Recovery Environment (WinRE) to kick off the cloud rebuild. If Windows can load, your computer should automatically enter WinRE mode, where you can then choose the cloud rebuild. You should need to make sure your PC is online via a wired or wireless connection.
Other Windows 11 November upgrades
The November update also enhances or fixes other Windows features and apps.

File Explorer will now more clearly and consistently show you the names, locations, and dates of files when you search for them. Phone Link will preview the text in a recent message if you hover over it. The AutoPlay dialog box that appears when you connect a device like a phone or camera has been given a more modern makeover. The Privacy & security page in Settings now groups together related controls for easier viewing. Plus, there are changes to the Taskbar, Magnifier, Narrator, Xbox Mode, and Live Captions.
Windows 11 November update security fixes
And that then brings us to the security fixes.

This month’s update resolves 1,094 security vulnerabilities, according to Microsoft, with 63 of them rated critical and one already exploited in the wild. That’s fewer than October’s record of 1,400 patches. But it still represents a hefty number as Microsoft and other vendors continue to rely on AI to find and fix security holes.

The exploited flaw points to a spoofing vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook. Here, a remote attacker who sends you a malicious email and convinces you to open it could cause Outlook to connect to a network controlled by that attacker. In this case, though, you would not receive any warning. Further, the exploit might reveal your username and password to the sender, potentially allowing them to impersonate you.

articles.headline: What is the 'Dead Internet Theory' and should humanity be worried?
keyFacts: The dead internet theory posits that non-human activity and AI-generated content increasingly dominate the internet.
Thales reported that automated bots accounted for 53 percent of all web traffic in 2026.
Experts and studies note that bots can spread disinformation while 40 percent of Americans expect AI to negatively impact society.
body: What is the 'Dead Internet Theory' and should humanity be worried?

When spending time online today, do you ever get the feeling that digital life has become eerily less human? Perhaps social media posts seem a bit off, or you get the sneaking suspicion the customer service representative you are chatting with is actually a bot. If this sounds familiar, you aren't alone: a paradigm called the "dead internet theory" has been gaining momentum in the last several years, positing that the internet is increasingly dominated by non-human activity, including bots and AI-generated content.

Since the theory first started making the rounds on internet forums in the 2010s, AI has only gotten more powerful. In September 2026, OpenAI reported that it had found a solution to a famously difficult mathematics puzzle, the Navier-Stokes problem. Meanwhile, a 2026 report from cybersecurity group Thales found that automated traffic continues to overtake human activity online, with bots accounting for 53 percent of all web traffic, up from 51 percent the year before. And bots are now talking to each other without humans in the loop at all: In March, Meta acquired Moltbook — a social network on which AI chatbots communicate with one another, often discussing humans. So as the internet landscape potentially gets less human every day, what exactly is dead internet theory, where does it come from, and should we be worried?
What is the dead internet theory?

Dead Internet Theory — the idea that the majority of the internet is propelled by bots and other non-human agents – has been floating around for quite some time. It first emerged as a conspiracy theory on internet forums in the late 2010s, but gained a more concrete framework following a post in 2021 on online community Agora Road titled, "Dead Internet Theory: Most of the Internet Is Fake," which argued "the Internet feels empty and devoid of people." Followers of the theory argued that the internet "died" around 2016 when search engines and social media feeds started surfacing more AI-generated content.

The popularity of chatbots and AI-generated content has only further expanded since then. In 2024, only 33 percent of Americans said they had used chatbots like ChatGPT, Gemini or Copilot, a study from Pew Research found. By 2026, that number had increased to nearly half of Americans at 49 percent. That same report found that 25 percent of Americans use chatbots every day. In many realms of society we are now facing chatbot loops: in schools, students are writing essays using AI, which teachers then grade with AI. In the job search, employees use chatbots to spit out optimized resumes and cover letters which are then analyzed by AI systems. Increasingly, humans are cut out of the conversation entirely, our voices replaced with bots.
Should we be worried?

On a personal level, this chatbot loop can feel uncanny. Those script-like posts we see on LinkedIn or a soulless AI-generated poster at your local cafe can induce a feeling of existential dread, but the consequences go beyond personal discomfort. Bots can spread disinformation that causes real harm. AI chatbots are increasingly a source of election disinformation, and little is being done legislatively to regulate this new frontier, though government agencies have issued warnings on deepfakes and other AI-powered risks to free elections.

As AI use grows, so has the backlash: 40 percent of Americans say they think AI will have a negative impact on society in the next 20 years, according to a Pew Research study. AI detection is becoming increasingly popular, with company Pangram receiving $9 million in backing in July 2026 for its AI detection system. Following the passage of the EU AI Act, OpenAI has started watermarking AI-generated content. With measures like these, people opposed to AI will hopefully be able to more easily spot and avoid the artificial slop in favor of the human-centric connection they initially came to the internet to find.

articles.headline: California just voted to give two billionaires $4 billion in taxpayer money so they can do obscure research
keyFacts: California voters approved Proposition 38, authorizing the state to sell $8.4 billion in bonds for medical research.

Supporters said the measure will fund immunology research and offset federal funding cuts, while opponents criticized it for benefiting a billionaire-founded nonprofit and saddling the state with debt.
Half of the funds will go to a single nonprofit co-founded by Gary Michelson and Meyer Luskin, while the rest will be distributed through competitive grants.
body: California voters have approved a eyebrow-raising ballot measure to support medical research that will send more than $4 billion in taxpayer money to a nonprofit founded by a pair of billionaires.

Proposition 38 — dubbed “the worst California proposition” by a columnist for the San Francisco Chronicle — officially passed with more than 54% support and 83% of the vote counted, according to the Associated Press.

“The measure will fund a statewide network of researchers, universities and nonprofit institutions working to advance immunology discoveries and turn promising science into life-saving treatments,” the Yes on 38 campaign said in a statement Monday.
Sign up for the California Morning Report newsletter
The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.
Thanks for signing up!
“Its passage comes as federal research funding cuts have disrupted clinical trials and delayed medical discoveries nationwide.”
The low-profile ballot measure, which will authorize the state to sell $8.4 billion in bonds to fund medical research at state institutes and universities, has turned some heads.

Half of the money will be directed to a single nonprofit immunology research institute affiliated with the University of California, with the remaining funds distributed through competitive grants to public and nonprofit research institutions.

That UC institute getting half the cash is the yet-open California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy at University of California, Los Angeles, co-founded by philanthropist and medical inventor Gary Michelson businessman Meyer Luskin.
The billionaires launched the institute and Michelson was the primary backer of Prop 38, contributing more than $65 million to the campaign, the Sacramento Bee reported.
Download The California Post App, follow us on social, and subscribe to our newsletters
That sparked criticism from opponents, who accused Michelson of funneling taxpayer money to his own organization, which is reportedly is still understaffed.

“Something stinks about two billionaires getting taxpayers to pay for their pet project, especially when the measure doesn’t disclose that,” Consumer Watchdog wrote in its endorsement picks of California’s propositions.
The California Post reached out to Michelson through the institute for comment.

Opponents of Prop 38 also argued that it’s unfair for money to be directed to just one area of medical research when so many have been impacted by federal cuts. They also claim that the measure could saddle the state with debt.
According to legislative analysis, the state will have to pay $500 million to $600 million annually for 20 years to repay the Prop 38 bond.
Critics pointed out as well that there will be a statutory exemption for the institute from public sector transparency laws.

“California deserves a funding process designed to maximize the likelihood of finding cures, with strong accountability and research proposals judged on their scientific merits,” the No on Proposition 38 campaign said in a Tuesday statement.
“We believe Californians would have rejected Proposition 38 on its merits had they had sufficient time and information to understand its deep flaws.”
Any medications developed from research supported by the bond funding will have to be sold at a 20% discount to Californians, and 10% of any revenue will go back to the state.

articles.headline: What to know about the Republican-led effort to impeach Pete Hegseth
keyFacts: Republican Representative Thomas Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
The articles accuse Hegseth of unauthorized war actions, unlawful military strikes, and suppressing free speech.
House procedural votes and impeachment votes are scheduled to move quickly.
body: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) speaks during a press conference on articles of impeachment against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, outside the US Capitol in Washington, DC, on November 9, 2026. | Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth may be on track to become just the third Cabinet member in history to be impeached, after Republican Rep. Thomas Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment against him on Monday.

Some articles of impeachment, which accuse Hegseth of high crimes and misdemeanors, focus on Hegseth’s conduct during the Iran war, including waging war without congressional authorization. Others accuse Hegseth of carrying out unlawful military strikes against boats carrying alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean and the Pacific, suppressing free speech, kidnapping former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro , and waging unlawful war in Yemen.

The articles are poised to move quickly in the House, with a procedural vote set for Tuesday evening and impeachment votes following as soon as Wednesday. Republicans still hold a slim House majority until January following last week’s Democratic tsunami in the midterm elections — but it’s possible that enough of them could join with Massie and House Democrats to impeach Hegseth anyway.

Hegseth, so far, has been defiant. On Tuesday, he defended his tenure atop the Pentagon in a rare press conference, calling the impeachment effort a “political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment.”
Following the press conference, President Donald Trump posted online that Hegseth deserves an “A PLUS PLUS PLUS” for defending himself.

To figure out what awaits for Hegseth and what it could mean for the Iran war, Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram spoke with the Washington Post’s Dan Lamothe about the impeachment effort, how the Pentagon is feeling after eight months of the Iran war, and whether there’s an off-ramp in sight.

Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify .
What are the vibes in the Pentagon in Washington, DC? Did the Iran war lose Republicans these midterms?
I don’t think it is the only deciding factor, but I think it is a significant factor in two ways.

One, there is a group of Republicans who voted for Donald Trump because he said he would not get us into any more protracted wars. The Iran war is eight months and counting. There seems to be no easy off-ramps even now. We’re not really fully at war. We’re certainly not at peace.

And as a result, the second issue — affordability, cost of living — a significant deciding factor in that is the price of gasoline, which then affects the price of groceries and everything else. So yes, there is a direct line between the war and a lot of the issues that were a factor.

A lot of Democrats have been saying that they want to impeach Pete Hegseth if they take control. Now they will. Future [House] Speaker Hakeem Jeffries came out this weekend and said that he’s into the idea. Remind us, why Hegseth?
I think there’s a couple of things going on. One, you’re likely to see an impeachment vote this week: the Rep. Thomas Massie-led effort to impeach.

There are a lot of angry Democrats, obviously, but there are a number of Republicans likely to cross the aisle on this and it may very well pass the House. I don’t know if it’s going to pass the Senate. That seems like a much bigger leap.

Either way, you’ve got an on-the-record rebuke, and you also have a forcing function to get every single member either on the record voting for it or on the record that they avoided voting for it. So that’s going to be a messy situation.
What are the actual grounds for impeachment of Hegseth?

On the Iran issue, it’s a little more complicated because you can think the policy of going into the war with Iran is problematic, detrimental to the national security of the country based on the amount of munitions we’re using, a variety of things. There’s not necessarily anything straight-up illegal in that.
Where I think they’re going to dig in is, they’re going to say that Iran went [on] longer than you’re allowed without having any kind of authorization.
Hegseth appears to be kicking off some sort of PR campaign in defense of his tenure. Is that just for the president or is that for Congress as well?

I think it’s primarily for the president. I do think there is a secondary audience of members on the Hill — Republicans on the Hill in particular — who are not sure how to handle this going forward. But I think foremost, this was meant for the president. It was very Trump-esque in terms of its feel. It had a defiance to it. It had a grievance in it and it had the feel of, they’re coming after me and I’m not going anywhere .
I initially was like, this feels like that scene in Wolf of Wall Street where Leonardo DiCaprio says, “I’m not leaving.”
And then within a day — I guess I should have seen it coming — the White House put out a video with a series of clips in it and sure enough, that was one of the clips. So that’s the vibe.

Even last week, when we saw Susie Wiles get pushed out at the White House as President Trump’s [new] chief of staff — Stephen Miller is much closer with Hegseth and you saw messaging from both sides, both the Pentagon and the White House, making the point that Hegseth continues to enjoy the support of both Stephen Miller and Donald Trump.
And I think we’re all left wondering, does that continue into the new year with Democratic majorities in both chambers of the Congress at that point?
How does it feel inside the Pentagon right now? What is the state of the war at this point?
I think there’s exhaustion.

Not unlike some of the other earlier wars that we’ve covered, you go in with good intentions, you go in with a goal, there’s markers up on the board, there’s a campaign plan. And then at some point when it starts to go wrong, you can explain away some of the earlier problems. But the challenge is over time, when you say, “Hey, we won back in April,” and yet you still have vessels getting hit all the time.

The Strait of Hormuz, they say it’s open. There are still vessels getting through, but it’s under duress. There’s still missile fire coming at a lot of vessels. This is not easy. This is not going normally. Everything is a drain.

There has been an increasing finger-pointing within the government, within the military where people say, “Hey, Hegseth is a participant in this. He’s a player in this.” There is at least a discussion of whether or not the president got the information he should have got, whether or not there was some gilding of the lily there in terms of what the US military could effectively do.

And I think there are military officers there who are caught in the middle. Do you gussy it up on the front end or leave out some of the information that’s a little difficult for the president to digest in the first weeks of the war? And is that a factor on where we are now?
Is anyone seriously talking about just ending this very unpopular quagmire situation of a war we’ve got in Iran?

Certainly people are talking about it. And I think how you get there is the challenge in it. I think when you’re looking at things like whether or not to strike again, are we talking one big night, a couple of days?

Most of the people I’m talking to who are tracking this issue that are still in government say they can’t do this for weeks on end. So this is not going to be a return to what we saw in March and April.

There are people telling the president, “Quit now, declare victory and get out.” There are people telling the president, “Do these handful of things, then declare victory and get out.” And there are other people that say, “Keep going.”

Who wins that argument? I think it remains to be seen. And that’s one of the reasons that you had the election landslide you had, because now you’re going to have pressure from the Congress in a way you simply have not for the last two years.

articles.headline: Senate GOP rebellion fizzles as Thune keeps power despite historic midterm massacre
keyFacts: Senate Majority Leader John Thune secured another term despite a push by some Republicans to delay the leadership elections following midterm losses.
Sen. Ron Johnson led an unsuccessful effort to delay the vote to discuss midterm election results and future strategy, losing on a 31 to 15 vote.
Thune and his leadership team were swiftly elected after closed-door conversations and without opposition to any of the lawmakers running for leadership.
body: There was neither an exodus nor a mass housecleaning in the Senate GOP leadership, despite frustration and rumblings of discontent among some lawmakers reeling from last week’s devastating midterm losses.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., secured another term as the top Republican behind the closed doors of the Old Senate Chamber, where lawmakers charted their course for their few remaining weeks in power and beyond.
Thune, along with the bulk of his leadership team, which now includes Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, were swiftly elected after a group of Republicans failed to delay the leadership elections.
It wasn't without a fight, though, with conversations behind closed doors dragging on for over seven hours.
GOP SENATOR WITHHOLDS SUPPORT FOR THUNE AS LEADERSHIP SHOWDOWN LOOMS
Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., led the charge to delay, and didn't stick around after his attempts to do so failed on a 31 to 15 vote in the Old Senate Chamber to proceed with the scheduled election.

Johnson and others wanted to have a deep conversation about what had happened during the midterm elections, and a roadmap on what Republican leadership candidates could accomplish with the little time they had left in power.
SENATE GOP REBELS MOVE TO DELAY LEADERSHIP VOTE, DEMAND RECKONING AFTER MIDTERM DISASTER
But there was no opposition to any of the lawmakers running for leadership.

"This has never been anything against John Thune," Johnson said. "I think he has been very unfairly attacked, you know, by our base, and I don't agree with that. What I didn't agree with was holding the election right away, giving nobody an opportunity to really challenge any leadership position."
On Monday, Thune was adamant that he’d still run but was unsure of the outcome.
"That's the hope," Thune said when asked if he had the Senate GOP’s support. "You never know right until they vote."
Before the vote, Johnson and a handful of others believed there should be a shakeup in leadership, but didn’t offer an alternative to Thune.
"After the stunning defeat, you just can't continue on business as usual," Johnson said. "I mean, that kind of defeat demands change."
When asked if he’d be interested in running, Johnson said, "That’s part of the problem. Would you want it?"

"I think there's a number of people with talent," Johnson said. "Again, I'm not — at a minimum, we need to see out of our leadership team what's the strategy moving forward, and you can't come off of a defeat like that and just ram through elections and oh yeah, ‘let's just elect that leadership team by acclamation.’"

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., had previously run for leader twice and most recently against Thune. But the lawmaker, who joined Johnson’s crusade for change, declined to throw his hat into the arena again.
"I think we have to acknowledge the voters are not happy," Scott said. "We have to start listening to voters."
CONGRESS RETURNS TO BRUTAL LAME-DUCK STRETCH WITH SHUTDOWN DEADLINE, LEADERSHIP RACES: 'CLOSET IS FULL OF S—'

Scott wanted ironclad promises on the GOP’s to-do list, including ramming through judicial nominees, government funding "without a massive omnibus," a stock trade ban, permitting reform, passing the National Defense Authorization Act, taking another crack at the SAVE America Act and balancing the budget — possibly through budget reconciliation.

Johnson and Scott were joined by Sens. Ted Budd, R-N.C., Mike Lee, R-Utah, John Kennedy, R-La., Jim Banks, R-Ind., and Dave McCormick, R-Pa., in a push to delay the elections that was not met, and the would-be coup faded as the secret ballots were cast.

Still, there were others outside that cohort who weren’t happy with last week and believed that there should be deeper soul-searching on what Republicans did over the last two years that led to a historic night for Senate Democrats.
Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., contended that much of what the GOP listed as accomplishments over their time in power is what worked against them.
"And, you know, you have the kind of record that this Congress has had, I think we better have a pretty tough family conversation about what it is we're doing," Hawley said.

"When you cut Medicaid, but you fund data centers, when you cut rural hospital funding, but you fund Planned Parenthood, when you let the cost of healthcare for working people go through the roof, but you can't do anything for them on other issues of affordability, from fertilizer to gas," he continued. "Yeah you know what? The public doesn’t like that very much."

articles.headline: To thwart reverse engineering by agents, dev proposes blinding them
keyFacts: Software developer Timo Zhang created Blind LLM Agents (BLA) to protect shipped application code from being reverse-engineered by AI agents.
Zhang stated that BLA hardens built software using techniques like renaming, string encryption, and decoys to increase the cost of analysis.
Zhang acknowledged that BLA adds friction rather than providing unbreakable protection, and it does not stop traditional reverse-engineering tools.
body: Now that LLMs can help analyze commercial software binaries and recreate their functionality, one software developer and student has created a project designed to make this process more difficult.
Timo Zhang's project is called Blind LLM Agents (BLA), and as its name suggests, it attempts to interfere with efforts by AI agents to scrutinize app code.

"Coding agents can reverse-engineer shipped packages, CLIs, and WASM in minutes," Zhang told The Register in an email. "Classic obfuscation was built for humans and static tools, not LLMs that reason about meaning. Blind LLM Agents is a protection layer for that threat model."
Such agents can also help developers build alternatives to existing commercial software.

Last month, Artcraft , a two-person development shop, released seven open-source apps that aim to be replacements for Adobe's commercial apps Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere Pro, Lightroom, After Effects, InDesign, and Acrobat Pro. Artcraft claims these apps are "clean-room reimplementations" written from scratch in Rust using Anthropic Opus 5.5.

Setting aside the question of whether enlisting an AI model to reimplement an app really immunizes the creator from legal risk, those making apps face the possibility that someone will have an LLM probe published app binaries and reconstruct them through reverse engineering. There's in fact a framework for this, Reverse Engineer Anything (REA).

Zhang has faced some criticism on social media for creating a limited barrier to copying other people's work (which at this point might simply be the work of another LLM). But not everyone accepts that all publicly accessible binaries should be easily available for review and reuse. BLA cannot prevent committed reverse engineering efforts, but it may add a bit of friction to the process when LLMs are involved.

"It doesn't write app code — it hardens what you've already built," Zhang said. "A transform pipeline (plus MCP tools / an agent Skill) applies renaming, lane splitting, seed-derived string encryption, build polymorphism, WASM export renaming, decoys, self-seal integrity checks, and a coverage matrix that won't claim protection it can't prove. Behavior stays equivalent; recovery cost goes up."
Zhang said various evaluations like red teaming and CrackMe challenges to recover keys or flags from hardened artifacts show that BLA is effective.

"We also drive REA (a reverse-engineering agent) against those builds," he said. "Fail-to-break is the pass. CI tracks defense score, self-verifies integrity coverage, and checks functional equivalence. We raise the cost — we don't claim it is unbreakable."

The project website says as much, noting that it raises the effort for analysis and adds decoy code, but doesn't promise protection against traditional interactive reverse engineering tools like Ghidra or Frida.

Zhang said he's aware of other software projects that aim to interfere with AI, such as Poison Fountain for poisoning training data and Anubis for deterring bots and scraping. BLA, he said, is different. It's for hardening shipping code against reverse engineering and LLM-aided analysis. ®

articles.headline: Senior U.S. Army soldier arrested in U.K. on suspicion of assisting Russian intelligence
keyFacts: British police said a senior U.S. Army soldier was arrested in the U.K. on suspicion of assisting Russian intelligence.
Sources told NBC News the 41-year-old man was based at NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps headquarters near Gloucester.
British counter terrorism policing stated that the investigation into the espionage allegations is ongoing.
body: LONDON — A senior U.S. Army soldier was arrested in the U.K. on suspicion of assisting Russian intelligence, British police said Tuesday.

The 41-year-old man was arrested “as part of an investigation by Counter Terrorism Policing” near the city of Gloucester, in the west of England, London’s Metropolitan Police said in a statement, adding that he remained in custody at a police station in the British capital.

He was arrested on suspicion of offences under sections 1 and 3 of the National Security Act, the statement said. These relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service.
“The country to which the allegations relate is Russia,” the statement added.
Three people familiar with the matter told NBC News that the soldier was based at NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps headquarters at Imjin Barracks on the outskirts of Gloucester.

FBI Director Kash Patel was quoted in the statement as saying that the arrest was “important” and “involves allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies.”
The FBI, he added, “has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners.”
Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, was also quoted in the police statement.
“The alleged conduct of a senior solider, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent,” he said.

“This case demonstrates the strength of our partnerships and the resolve of the counterintelligence community,” he added. “I am grateful to the U.K. and the FBI for their professionalism and teamwork throughout this investigation.”
Calling the allegations “very serious,” Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, Britain’s senior national coordinator for counter terrorism policing, said the “investigation is very much ongoing.”
The investigation is not linked to any other ongoing counter terror operations, the statement said.

But the arrest comes at a time of heightened tensions around the threat from hostile states, with British security services saying Russia and Iran have both used proxies to commit crimes on U.K. soil.

Officials in the U.K. have said proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arsons and other attacks in Britain and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear.
The United States has moved military aircraft from an airbase in the United Kingdom amid threats from Iran.
A U.S. official confirmed to NBC News that several military aircraft had left RAF Mildenhall as the security posture there had increased.
At least eight air refueling tankers and three Ospreys left the base in Suffolk, eastern England, on Monday, flight tracking data showed.

articles.headline: U.S. boycotts U.N. human rights review for second year running
keyFacts: The United States boycotted a United Nations human rights review for the second consecutive year, becoming the only member state to do so twice.
ACLU human rights director Jamil Dakwar stated that the administration continued to violate human rights regarding immigrants, protesters, and the LGBTQ community.
The United Nations postponed deliberations on how to handle the U.S. absence until early next year.
body: U.S. boycotts U.N. human rights review for second year running
GENEVA, Switzerland — The United States has left an empty chair at a key United Nations human rights review for the second year running, becoming the only U.N. member state ever to do so.

The review, known as the universal periodic review, is meant to be just that: universal. Each state is reviewed every four to five years by fellow member states. The aim is to ensure that every country, however powerful, undergoes a peer review of its human rights record.
As well as diplomats from countries under review, civil society groups are allowed to submit evidence too. Several made the trip to Geneva, led by the American Civil Liberties Union.

Jamil Dakwar, the ACLU's human rights director, told journalists that the current U.S. administration was continuing to violate human rights "unabashed," citing the treatment of immigrants, student protesters and the LGBTQ community as examples.

Dakwar said the U.N. must hold the U.S. accountable, warning that the Trump administration wanted to "dismantle human rights." In a written response, the State Department pointed out that Washington had already formally withdrawn from the U.N. Human Rights Council, accusing it of "pushing anti-American rhetoric."

In fact, leaving the council, which has 47 elected members, does not mean the U.S. can easily get out of the review process, which is obligatory for all 193 U.N. member states. Human rights groups see Washington's stance as part of a pattern of disengagement and even active opposition to multilateral organizations, pointing to U.S. sanctions on the International Criminal Court and the decision to leave the World Health Organization.

So what happens now? The U.N. has few sanctions against a country that does not cooperate with the review process. Israel skipped one review back in 2013 in protest at what it said was anti-Israel bias, but returned nine months later after the U.N. rescheduled. Until today's no-show by the U.S., no country has ever failed to turn up twice.

Rights groups would like the U.N. to hold the review anyway, and take evidence about alleged violations in the U.S. Member states had already drawn up a list of questions for Washington's diplomats, including questions about the use of the death penalty and restrictions on abortion.

But U.N. insiders fear that holding the review when there is no one to answer those questions could set a risky precedent. Even authoritarian regimes such as North Korea take part in the review process. If the U.N. allows a review to go ahead without U.S. participation, it could encourage other member states to stay away, too, leaving rights groups to present their evidence, as one put it, "in a vacuum."

For now, the U.N. has decided to postpone tricky deliberations about how to react until early next year. In the meantime, a process regarded as a last resort for the victims of human rights violations is not available to U.S. citizens. It is, one rights activist said in Geneva, "a crisis of accountability."

articles.headline: The Monaco summit that will decide the future of Carrick and Man Utd
keyFacts: Manchester United executives Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox are meeting in Monaco to discuss head coach Michael Carrick's future at the club.
Berrada and Wilcox are expected to recommend sacking Carrick following Manchester United's poor start which leaves them 18th in the Premier League.
Carrick will continue managing training sessions until he is told otherwise by the club.
body: - Published
Michael Carrick's future as Manchester United head coach will be determined 800 miles away from Old Trafford in Monaco on Wednesday.
Chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox are flying out for one of their regular pre-planned meetings to discuss strategy around the football club.
On this occasion, the main issue to be decided is Carrick's future and what should happen next.
It is expected that Berrada and Wilcox's recommendation is for the head coach to go.
It is not a situation Sir Jim Ratcliffe can have expected to find himself in again, less than three years after purchasing a minority stake in United.
On Christmas Eve 2023, his vision was much different.
"Our shared ambition is clear: we all want to see Manchester United back where we belong, at the very top of English, European and world football," he said.

Instead, United are 18th, in the Premier League's relegation zone after winning just one of their first 10 games and none since August. It is their lowest position so far into a top-flight season since 1986-87 when they were 20th.
Ratcliffe has been criticised for many decisions since he bought his 28.94% stake for just over Â£1bn. This is one he really needs to get right.
Why is the meeting taking place in Monaco?
Ratcliffe's home is in Monaco and his company Ineos has offices in the principality.
The meeting had been in the diary for some time as a regular catch-up between senior executives and their boss.
Sources have stressed that the choice of location was not influenced by the debate around Carrick's future - it just happens to now be the most important item for discussion.
The decision to sack United's previous two managers was not made in a meeting in Monaco.
Ruben Amorim was sacked 19 hours after his explosive media conference following a 1-1 draw at Leeds in January.
Erik ten Hag went a day after Manchester United lost at West Ham leaving them with just three wins from their opening nine matches

A decision to sack Dutchman Ten Hag was taken at a meeting of senior Ineos executives in the summer of 2024, only for the choice to be reversed following the FA Cup final triumph over Manchester City.
Four months later there was a six-hour meeting at Ineos HQ in London as Ten Hag's tenure hung by a thread. He survived again but was gone three weeks later.
Amorim was summoned to Monaco after the Europa League final defeat to Tottenham in 2025.

There is daily contact between senior executives so if the meeting was purely to decide Carrick's fate, it could be done by video conference and the need to travel to Monaco is not the reason why there is yet to be a decision.
The travel element does add a complication given the preference for Berrada and Wilcox is to inform Carrick of any decision face to face.
Sources say the Monaco meetings used to be held every six weeks, although in more recent times they are less frequent.
Those who have attended them say they take place in the morning, tend to last between three and four hours and usually stop on time so Ratcliffe can go for his regular lunchtime jog.
What do we know about the recommendation to sack Carrick?
United stood by Carrick after the woeful 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth on 25 October.

Club sources were adamant they wanted to give Carrick and his players a chance to turn the situation around it was also felt that the two-week international break in November represented a better chance for the club to properly assess the club's start to the campaign.
However, although they did end a long wait for a victory against Roma on 3 November, United had to come from two goals down to seal a 3-2 victory in a chaotic game.
They failed to press home their advantage after excelling in the first half against Chelsea and eventually lost 2-0 as experienced central defender Lisandro Martinez was sent off.
On Sunday, they conceded twice inside five minutes and had to come from two goals down twice to claim a point against Villa.

While sources said the comebacks showed the United squad were still playing for Carrick, it is also understood the chaotic nature of the games and the inability to stop the opposition from scoring has led Berrada and Wilcox, who were at all three matches, to conclude a change of coach is required to get United out of the mess they find themselves in.
United have conceded 30 goals so far this season in 15 games - 19 in 10 Premier League matches, eight in four in the Champions League and three in their one Carabao Cup tie.
Instead of replacing Carrick another option under consideration is additional coaching support to assist the current team.
Bayern Munich coach Aaron Danks, who worked with Carrick at Middlesbrough and was touted as a potential appointment in the summer, is one option.
Is the recommendation likely to be accepted?
The assumption is yes.
If Ratcliffe was to decide otherwise, it would raise serious questions over the future of Berrada and Wilcox.
How could they work with Carrick again in that scenario?

The pair have been the subject of intense and frequent fan discontent. But sources are adamant that Ratcliffe still retains faith in the pair, even though United are heading towards sacking a manager in mid-season for the third successive year, having backed them in the summer and spend millions on new players.

Ratcliffe is a ruthless operator, and has clear opinions of his own. He also has form, spending Â£5m hiring Dan Ashworth as sporting director from Newcastle in 2024, then waiting for the 55-year-old to spend five months on gardening leave before he could start work.

Five months later, Ashworth was sacked due to a divergence of opinion over who should replace Ten Hag. Ashworth felt someone with Premier League experience was a better fit for United's squad. Ratcliffe wanted a more modern alternative. Berrada suggested Amorim. Wilcox, after initial reservations, also got on board. Amorim was dismissed after 14 months.
The other unknown element is the Glazer family. They will need to sign off any decision.

At the time of the Ratcliffe purchase, United confirmed the club's 'board' had handed over responsibility for the football side. But United's articles of association state that responsibilities delegated by directors can also be "revoked or altered".

Crucially, of the 12 current directors, six are members of the Glazer family, including co-chairs Joel and Avi Glazer. United's rules state that if required, the chairman of any meeting will have a second and casting vote.
Although there have been media reports of Glazer dissatisfaction at United's current plight, there has been no public statement on the matter.
What is Carrick scheduled to be doing for the next couple of days?
It may seem strange, but the reality is, as with any employee, Carrick will continue to do his job until told otherwise - and so far, there has been no conversation to that effect.
Although most of his squad, and a significant number of academy players, are on international duty, a core remains at home.

This includes Mason Mount, Joshua Zirkzee and Matthijs de Ligt. Harry Maguire, who suffered a back spasm against Villa, is also there, as are other injured players, including Luke Shaw and Marcus Rashford.

Carrick gave his players a day off on Monday but scheduled training days for Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday. After that, they are not due to report back until 17 November, by which time the international contingent should start to return and begin preparations for the trip to Liverpool on 22 November.

"Obviously some of the boys will be flying off around the world and different things, and the group will be split for 10 days or so, but as a normal international week is, we'll have some training and we'll have one or two days off," Carrick said after the Villa game. "Not too much. But we'll train and get ready for the next game."
Who might be discussed as a possible replacement for Carrick?
If the discussions go as anticipated, replacing Carrick will be a key element.
Mauricio Pochettino has emerged as a leading contender and is known to be keen on the job.

United spoke to the former Tottenham, PSG and Chelsea boss about their managerial position on three different occasions - first of all when Jose Mourinho was sacked in 2018, then in 2022 when the club decided on Ten Hag instead and then again when the Dutchman was sacked.

The obvious problem is that Pochettino currently has a job as head coach of the United States. He renewed his contract in August and has a two-legged Concacaf Nations League quarter-final against Haiti over the next week. The Argentine, 54, is due to speak to the media on Friday and has a $10m (Â£7.5m) release clause.

Former Newcastle boss Eddie Howe is out of work and available. BBC Sport has reported the compensation due to his old club if Manchester United appointed thr 48-year-old now would be Â£3m. But it reduces as the season goes on and would be nothing in the summer.

Italian Antonio Conte is also thought to be keen and the 57-year-old has Premier League title-winning experience at Chelsea and more recently won Serie A with Napoli last season, before leaving the club.
Julian Nagelsmann stood down as Germany boss in the wake of their last-32 exit at the World Cup exit at the World Cup but the German, 39, won the Bundesliga title with Bayern Munich in 2022-23.

Kieran McKenna was part of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer's coaching team at Manchester United and left Ipswich after four-and-a-half years this summer. However, it is felt more likely United would want a candidate with greater experience than the 40-year-old Northern Irishman.
Where does this all leave Carrick? In a unenviable position of carrying on as if it was business as usual when the reality is anything but.

articles.headline: Trump says he sees no reason to escalate war with Iran
keyFacts: President Trump stated that he currently sees no reason to escalate the war with Iran, though Secretary of State Marco Rubio said talks are not close to a breakthrough because Iranian demands are unacceptable.

A British naval agency reported that a tanker was attacked and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz, while Saudi Arabia's energy ministry reported a limited fire on its East-West Crude Oil Pipeline after a targeted attack.
French officials accused a cyber unit of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of carrying out nationwide hacks on commercial refrigeration in October, causing food spoilage and fires.
body: What to know about the Iran war today:

- In a that aired Sunday, President Trump said he does not currently see "any reason" to escalate the . However, he defended starting the conflict as "historically" a good decision, despite its economic impact.
- Mr. Trump is meeting Monday with the prime minister of , whose country has mediated indirect talks between the U.S. and Iran aimed at reaching a deal.
- Secretary of State Marco Rubio curbed expectations late Sunday, saying talks are not "at the verge of a breakthrough" because Iran's demands are "unacceptable"
Hegseth says he's not worried about impeachment
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said he's not worried about a vote on articles of impeachment that could happen in the House as early as this week.
"We're not worried about that," Hegseth told reporters Monday.
He said he planned to hold a news conference on the impeachment effort Tuesday morning.
Tanker attacked in Strait of Hormuz over the weekend, British naval agency says
A tanker that was ablaze in the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday was attacked, a British naval agency said Monday.

In a post on X, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations center said that military authorities had reported the vessel was on fire, forcing the crew to evacuate, and that it had reclassified the incident as an attack.
The incident took place 8 nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman.
UKMTO did not give any details on the potential perpetrator or the vessel.

Meanwhile, Iran's state broadcaster IRIB said Monday that four tankers had been halted in the Strait of Hormuz over the preceding 24 hours. In a post on X, IRIB said the ships were "brought to a standstill," without offering any further detail.
Both Iran and the U.S. have attacked ships in and around the Strait of Hormuz that they consider to be breaching their respective restrictions on the waterway.
Saudi Arabia's East-West Crude Oil Pipeline targeted again, energy ministry says

Saudi Arabia's crucial East-West Crude Oil Pipeline has been targeted again, the kingdom's energy ministry said Monday. In a post on X, the ministry said a "limited fire" broke out on a section of the pipeline in the Medina region, and that no deaths or injuries were reported.
There was also "no disruption to the pipeline's operations," the statement added.
An , which Saudi Arabia blamed on Iranian-backed militias in Iraq, put the pipeline out of action for several weeks.
Saudi authorities did not say who they suspected to have carried out Monday's attack on the pipeline.

Saudi Arabia is the top crude oil producer in the world besides the United States, and it has used the East-West pipeline as a vital workaround to export its products given insecurity for tankers in the Persian Gulf amid the U.S. war with Iran.
French officials accuse Iran of being behind store refrigerator and freezer hacks in October

French officials believe Iran was behind nationwide cyberattacks on commercial refrigeration in October, the Paris Prosecutor's office said Monday, accusing a cyber unit of Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of carrying out the costly hacks.

The Oct. 11 hacking attack , hitting "700 retail locations across France," according to the prosecutor's office, which said the attack caused "significant food spoilage and triggered roughly twenty fires" as the temperatures in refrigeration units shot up.
The attacks on the French grocery store chains were followed weeks later by affecting refrigerators and freezers at supermarkets in Belgium, Luxembourg and Sweden.
In August, sparked an ongoing investigation by the Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division, Thomas Hamilton, a public affairs officer for the department, told CBS News.
Top UAE official says complete resolution of U.S.-Iran war and regional stability unlikely for "long period"
A senior official from the United Arab Emirates said Monday that the U.S.-Iran war was unlikely to be decisively settled for a "long period."

Dr. Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to the president and a senior figure within the administration of the United Arab Emirates, said Iran was facing "one of the most serious challenges" in its history, with an ailing economy, pressure on its leadership and a "fundamental dispute" with the U.S. and international community over its nuclear capabilities.

"These factors make a comprehensive political settlement difficult," he said, referring to the ongoing war. "We should therefore prepare for a long period of uncertainty in which neither a decisive resolution nor a stable regional order can be taken for granted."
The UAE always opposed the war, he added in his remarks at the Abu Dhabi Strategic Debate event on Monday, according to a transcript provided by the Emirati foreign ministry.

"Our assessment was guided by a fundamental understanding of the region. Wars begin through deliberate decisions, but their consequences rarely remain within the calculations of those who initiate them," he said.

Gargash said it was "perhaps too early to fully assess the impact of the U.S. midterm elections on Washington's approach toward Iran," and added that the UAE would "reinforce efforts to pursue diplomatic solutions that can ensure lasting peace and stability in the Gulf."
Beach closed due to oil spill on UAE coast just south of Strait of Hormuz

Authorities in the city of Khor Fakkan closed a beach Monday after an oil spill was found along the coastline of the United Arab Emirates city, which is only about 20 miles south of the Strait of Hormuz.
Reuters cited a notice posted by municipal authorities on social media announcing the closure, without providing any further details.

Numerous oil tankers and other commercial vessels have been attacked and disabled during the war by both Iran and the United States, each claiming to act in enforcement of their respective restrictions on the key shipping lanes of the Strait.

Most of the ships that have been hit by missiles or sea mines in the southern waters of the strait, in or near shipping lanes close to the Omani and UAE coasts, have been struck by Iran. Tehran rejects the southern routes endorsed by the U.S., warning ships against using the lanes and demanding that they instead transit the strait via northern routes closer to its coast.
Syria denies report of troops joining Saudi coalition to fight Yemen's Houthi rebels

Syria's foreign minister said Monday that his country has no troops deployed in Yemen and is not planning to send any. His remarks came several days after Yemeni sources told the French news agency AFP that Syrian soldiers were in Yemen and Saudi Arabia to support the Saudi-backed coalition fighting Iran's Houthi rebel allies.
"There is no deployment of troops to Yemen nor is there a plan for such deployment in the near future," Asaad al-Shaibani said at a Monday news conference.

AFP quoted Yemeni officials on Friday as saying thousands of Syrian troops were set to deploy to both countries, and that some were already there. The report cited an agreement reportedly reached during a meeting last week between Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman.
CBS/AFP
U.N. nuclear watchdog agency conducted inspection in Iran, foreign ministry says
The United Nations' international nuclear watchdog agency carried out an inspection of an Iranian nuclear site, the country's foreign ministry spokesperson said Monday.

Esmaeil Baqaei told Iranian journalists that the International Atomic Energy Agency conducted an inspection "a few days ago" in the city of Bushehr, which is home to the country's only civilian nuclear power plant.

President Trump has previously said he launched the war alongside Israel in February to prevent Iran from developing a nuclear weapon. Tehran, for its part, has repeatedly insisted it only uses nuclear materials for civilian purposes such as energy generation and medical work.
Iran suspended IAEA inspections at all of its facilities in the wake of on many sites by the U.S. and Israel.
Last week the U.S. military's Central Command announced a reward of up to $20 million for information about Iran's nuclear program.
Iran and U.S. continue to strike tankers in or near Strait of Hormuz

Iran's state broadcaster IRIB said Monday that four tankers had been "halted" in the Strait of Hormuz over the preceding 24 hours. In a post on X, IRIB said the ships were "brought to a standstill," without offering any further detail.
Both Iran and the U.S. have attacked ships in and around the Strait of Hormuz that they consider to be breaching their respective restrictions on the waterway.

Iran demands that all commercial vessels coordinate with its security forces to use shipping lanes in the north of the strait, close to its shores, and it has launched missiles at some it accuses of using southern routes that the U.S. insists are safe and open. Iranian authorities have claimed multiple times in recent weeks that ships using the southern routes have hit sea mines, causing fires.

The U.S. insists the southern routes are safe and open despite the ongoing attacks on ships using them, while American forces have attacked some commercial vessels accused of violating the U.S. military blockade of Iran's ports and vessels, intended to prevent the regime's sale of oil and gas.

On Saturday, U.S. Central Command said it disabled a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman, just east of the strait, after the crew "ignored repeated warnings and attempted to violate the naval blockade against Iran multiple times."
Oil prices continue cautious descent as Trump casts doubt on return to large-scale fighting with Iran

The price of Brent crude oil, the international standard, fell 2% early Monday morning to $96.38 per barrel, continuing a downward trend seen for more than a week as markets appeared to take hope from President Trump casting doubt on a return to full-scale war with Iran.
U.S. benchmark crude also fell, down 1.5% early Monday to $89.56 per barrel.

Oil prices have been up significantly since the U.S. and Israel launched the war with Iran, and Iran responded by attacking and threatening commercial ships in the key energy supply routes of the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz. They remain about 50% higher than a year ago, before the war began, but down from highs seen during the peak of fighting, when Brent crude soared to near $120 a barrel.
Iran calls its proposed shortening of the implementation period for potential peace deal a goodwill gesture

Iran's foreign ministry spokesman said Monday that Tehran's proposal to reduce the implementation period for a possible peace deal with the U.S. to two days from the previous seven was a "sign of goodwill."

Foreign Ministry Spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei told Iranian journalists that any deal with the U.S. must include the under the previous, so-called Islamabad agreement in June. That deal called for the lifting of U.S. sanctions on Iran as well as the U.S. naval blockade of Iran's ports, unfreezing Iranian assets and a ceasefire on all fronts in the Middle East.

"If the other side is genuinely even minimally serious, Iran can fulfill its own commitments within two days," he added. "We have already demonstrated that we are serious about fulfilling our commitments."
The previous ceasefire fell apart after several weeks, as Iran declared the continuation of the U.S. naval blockade a violation of its terms.
On Sunday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio downplayed the likelihood of an imminent deal with Iran, calling Tehran's demands "unacceptable."

The Trump administration has been pushing for Iran to agree to conditions on its nuclear program as part of an initial peace agreement, but Tehran has long insisted discussion on the topic can begin only after fighting and threats cease.
Rubio says U.S. and Iran not "at the verge of a breakthrough" on deal
Secretary of State Marco Rubio tempered expectations of an imminent deal between Iran and the U.S. late Sunday.
Before departing to Paris for a G7 meeting, Rubio said the two sides are not "at the verge of a breakthrough, while reiterating the president prefers a diplomatic solution.
"Right now, it hasn't been very productive because the Iranian demands are simply not just unacceptable," Rubio told reporters.
He said he expects G7 allies to have a lot of questions about the conflict and next steps.
CBS/AFP
Trump expected to meet with Qatari mediator
President Trump is to meet with Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani at the White House on Monday.
Qatar has been one of the key mediators in indirect talks between the U.S. and Iran aimed at reaching a deal to end the conflict.
According to sources cited by Axios, Al Thani, who is one of the key mediators in those talks, is looking to Mr. Trump to allow more time for diplomacy.
Trump says he sees no reason to escalate war on Iran
President Trump said in an interview aired on Sunday that he sees no reason to escalate the war on Iran and that he is "not looking" to do so.
"Well, I'm not looking to. I don't think there's any reason to," Mr. Trump told 60 Minutes when asked whether he was planning to intensify the war.
However, the president emphatically defended his decision to start the conflict in late February, while recognizing there have been negative impacts in the meantime.
"I think, historically, this will be a very good decision," Mr. Trump said. "Is it a good decision for today and tomorrow? Maybe not."
The president cited Iran's nuclear program as the main reason for starting the war, adding that he had done "what's right for our country."
See and read
Trump says new task force to extend naval blockade "is in full force and effect"
President Trump said Sunday that the new U.S. military task force to extend the Iran naval blockade "is in full force and effect."

"Task Force Iron Gate is in full force and effect in the Islamic Republic of Iran. Coupled with history's greatest Naval Blockade, very little gets into, or out of, Iran!" Mr. Trump said in a Truth Social post.
Task Force Iron Gate is aimed at extending the success of the naval blockade to overland routes of trade, U.S. Central Command announced Saturday.

The group will be tasked with preventing military technology and illegal revenue streams from entering or exiting Iranian borders, including via the Caspian Sea, but it was unclear if any military force would be brought to bear.
